title: Where it is, and what isn't there
goal: Say that something is or isn't there, ask where it is, describe position with place words, and learn the difference between 에 and 에서 from the very start.
bekal: use 있어요 and 없어요 for existence and possession
ask where something is with 어디에 있어요
describe position: on, under, in front of, next to
tell the particle 에 apart from 에서

dialogs.title: 대화 — Looking for a lost key
dialogs.intro: Ani can't find her room key. Notice that Korean place words come **after** the reference object — the reverse of English "on the desk", "under the chair".

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Minjun, do you have my key?

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: No. Isn't it in your bag?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: It's not there. It's not on the desk either.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Did you look under the chair?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Oh! Here it is! It's under the chair.
lines.literal: ah! here — exists! chair — under-at — exists.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: What a relief. By the way, where's the dictionary?
lines.literal: relief — is. by-the-way, dictionary — as-for — where-at — exists?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: It's in the classroom. On the desk.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Ani, where are you studying today?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: At the library. And you, Minjun?

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: I'm going home. I work from home.
lines.literal: I — as-for — home-to — go. home-at(place) — work.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: The library is next to the school. Shall we go together?
lines.literal: library — as-for — school — side-at — exists. together — go?

notes: **있어요 does two jobs at once.** It means "there is" (existence somewhere) and also "have" (possession). 열쇠 있어요? can mean "is the key there?" or "do you have a key?" — context decides. English separates the two; Korean doesn't feel the need.

**없어요 is not 안 있어요.** Korean has its own word for "there isn't", and the usual negative (안) isn't used here. The pair 있다/없다 keeps coming back until the last unit, including inside big expressions like "can" and "can't".

**Place words come AFTER the noun.** 책상 위 = "desk top" = on the desk. 가방 안 = "bag inside" = in the bag. It's the reverse of English prepositions and one of the things that feels odd the longest. Practice by naming things in your room: 침대 옆, 문 앞, 의자 밑.
**The place word itself is a noun, so it needs a particle.** 위 (top) plus 에 becomes 위**에**. Without 에 the sentence isn't finished: 책상 위 있어요 is wrong, 책상 위**에** 있어요 is right.
**여기, 거기, 저기** follow the same three-distance pattern as 이거/그거/저거: here (near me), there (near you), over there (far from both of us). To ask: 어디.

**다행이에요 has no one-word equivalent.** It's said when something bad turns out not to have happened — closest to "what a relief" or "thank goodness". It's very common, and sounds much warmer than 좋아요 in situations like this.

**그런데 opens a change of topic.** Literally "but", in conversation it more often means "by the way" — a gentle way of steering the conversation elsewhere. The short form is 근데, and that's what you'll hear most.
**같이 is pronounced *gachi*, not *gati*.** The letter ㅌ meeting 이 changes its sound to *chi*. This change has its own name (구개음화) and only happens with ㄷ and ㅌ before 이: 굳이 *guji*, 같이 *gachi*.

grammars.title: 에 vs 에서 — two place particles you must not mix up
body: English uses "at/in" for two things that Korean treats as completely different: **where something is** and **where something happens**. This is the number one particle mistake for learners, and it never goes away by itself — you have to notice it once and then practice.

head: Particle
Used for
Verbs it pairs with
Example
rows: 세 시**에** 만나요 — meet at three

after: **The one-sentence quick test: is some activity being done in that place?** If yes → 에서. If the place is only where something is, or where someone is going → 에.
Look at the pair in the dialogue: 집**에** 가요 (go home — movement) but 집**에서** 일해요 (work at home — activity). Same noun, different particle, very different meaning.
⚠️ The most common mistake: 식당**에** 먹어요. Eating is an activity, so the correct form is 식당**에서** 먹어요. If in doubt, remember that 에 only keeps company with 있다, 없다, 가다 and 오다.

grammars.title: Place words
body: All of them go after the reference noun and take 에.

head: Korean
Romanization
Meaning
Example
rows: 학교 앞에 — in front of the school
은행과 학교 사이에 — between the bank and the school

after: **밑 and 아래 both mean "under", but they're not quite the same.** 밑 means right underneath, touching or covered by it; 아래 is more general, meaning somewhere below. For a key that fell under a chair, 밑 is the right one.

**밖에 has a tricky second meaning.** Attached to a noun and followed by a negative, it means "only": 물**밖에** 없어요 = "there's nothing but water" = "there's only water". Spelled the same as "outside", but doing a completely different job.

blocks.text: The vocabulary that's useful fastest if you're actually in Korea, and that comes up most often in TOPIK level 1 questions.

blocks.title: 화장실이 어디예요?
items: This sentence is worth memorizing before any other. Notice that it uses **이/가**, not 은/는 — because you're asking the other person to pick out one place among many.
Notice too that it uses **예요**, not 있어요. 화장실이 어디예요? (where's the restroom?) and 화장실이 어디에 있어요? are both correct; the first is shorter and more common.
My key is in the bag.
The library is next to the school.

exercises.prompt: Fill in 있어요 or 없어요 according to the meaning.
items: It's in the bag: 가방 안에 ____.
It's not on the desk: 책상 위에 ____.
I have a Korean friend: 한국 친구가 ____.
I don't have any money: 돈이 ____.
The restroom is over there: 화장실은 저기에 ____.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
